_link.title: I can explain the structure of ATP and ADP and how energy is stored and released

options.text: Adenosine triphosphate
options.explanation: ATP stands for adenosine triphosphate, reflecting its structure of adenosine plus three phosphate groups.

options.text: Adenine tetraphosphate
options.explanation: ATP has three phosphate groups (tri-), not four (tetra-).

options.text: Active transport protein
options.explanation: ATP is a molecule, not a protein; it stands for adenosine triphosphate.

options.text: Amino acid triphosphate
options.explanation: ATP contains adenosine (adenine + ribose), not an amino acid.

toLevel2.stem: What are the components that make up adenosine in ATP?

options.text: Adenine and ribose sugar
options.explanation: Adenosine consists of the nitrogenous base adenine bonded to a ribose sugar.

options.text: Glucose and three phosphates
options.explanation: Glucose is not part of ATP; adenosine is made of adenine and ribose.

options.text: Thymine and deoxyribose sugar
options.explanation: Thymine and deoxyribose are components of DNA, not ATP.

options.text: Uracil and fructose sugar
options.explanation: Uracil is found in RNA; adenosine contains adenine and ribose.

toLevel2.stem: How many phosphate groups does ATP contain?

options.text: Three
options.explanation: ATP has three phosphate groups, which is indicated by 'tri' in triphosphate.

options.text: Two
options.explanation: Two phosphate groups would make ADP (adenosine diphosphate), not ATP.

options.text: One
options.explanation: One phosphate group would make AMP (adenosine monophosphate), not ATP.

options.text: Four
options.explanation: ATP contains three phosphate groups, not four.

toLevel2.stem: What is formed when ATP releases energy?

options.text: ADP and a phosphate group
options.explanation: When ATP loses its third phosphate group, it becomes ADP and releases energy.

options.text: Glucose and carbon dioxide
options.explanation: Glucose and CO₂ are related to respiration, not the direct breakdown of ATP.

options.text: Two molecules of ATP combined
options.explanation: ATP breaks down into ADP; it does not combine into a larger molecule.

options.text: Water and oxygen molecules
options.explanation: Water and oxygen are involved in respiration; ATP breakdown yields ADP and phosphate.

toLevel2.stem: How is ATP reformed from ADP?

options.text: A phosphate group is added back to ADP using available energy
options.explanation: When energy is available, a phosphate group is reattached to ADP to reform ATP.

options.text: ADP is broken down further into individual atoms and rebuilt
options.explanation: ADP is not broken down; a phosphate group is simply added back to it.

options.text: A new adenosine molecule is synthesised from raw materials
options.explanation: The adenosine component remains intact; only the phosphate group is added.

options.text: Two ADP molecules fuse together to create one ATP molecule
options.explanation: ATP is reformed by adding a single phosphate to one ADP, not by fusing two ADP molecules.

toLevel2.stem: Energy is released from ATP when the bond between the second and third phosphate group is broken.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Breaking the bond between the second and third phosphate releases energy and converts ATP to ADP.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement is correct; the energy is released from breaking this specific bond.

options.text: True
options.explanation: ADP stands for adenosine diphosphate, meaning it has two phosphate groups, not three.

options.text: False
options.explanation: ADP has two phosphate groups; ATP has three.

toLevel2.stem: ATP consists of {{blank:1}} bonded to three {{blank:2}} groups.

options.text: adenosine
options.explanation: Adenosine (adenine + ribose sugar) forms the base of the ATP molecule.

options.text: glucose
options.explanation: Glucose is a sugar used in respiration, not a component of ATP.

options.text: cytosine
options.explanation: Cytosine is a nitrogenous base found in DNA and RNA, not in ATP.

options.text: phosphate
options.explanation: ATP has three phosphate groups, hence the name triphosphate.

options.text: hydroxyl
options.explanation: Hydroxyl groups are not the energy-storing components of ATP.

options.text: carboxyl
options.explanation: Carboxyl groups are found in amino acids and fatty acids, not in ATP.

toLevel2.stem: When ATP is broken down, it forms {{blank:1}} and releases {{blank:2}} for cellular processes.

options.text: ADP and Pi
options.explanation: ATP loses one phosphate group (Pi) to become ADP.

options.text: glucose and CO₂
options.explanation: Glucose and CO₂ are involved in respiration, not the direct breakdown of ATP.

options.text: water and oxygen
options.explanation: Water and oxygen are not the products of ATP breakdown.

options.text: energy
options.explanation: Breaking the phosphate bond releases energy that powers cellular activities.

options.text: light
options.explanation: ATP breakdown releases chemical energy, not light energy.

options.text: heat only
options.explanation: While some heat is released, the primary purpose is to release usable chemical energy.

toLevel2.stem: The ATP–ADP cycle allows cells to {{blank:1}} energy when ATP is broken down and {{blank:2}} energy when ATP is reformed.

options.text: release
options.explanation: Energy is released when the phosphate bond in ATP is broken.

options.text: store
options.explanation: Energy is stored when ATP is reformed, not when it is broken down.

options.text: destroy
options.explanation: Energy is not destroyed; it is released for use by the cell.

options.text: store
options.explanation: Energy is stored in the bond when a phosphate group is added back to ADP.

options.text: release
options.explanation: Energy is released when ATP is broken down, not when it is reformed.

options.text: absorb
options.explanation: While energy is input, the correct term in this context is that energy is stored in the reformed ATP.

toLevel3.stem: Why is ATP often described as the energy currency of the cell?

options.text: It can be quickly broken down and reformed to transfer energy where needed
options.explanation: Like currency, ATP is a convenient, universal carrier that can be spent (broken down) and earned (reformed) rapidly.

options.text: It is stored permanently in the cell and never recycled or reused at all
options.explanation: ATP is continuously recycled; it is not stored permanently.

options.text: It can only be used once and must be made from scratch each time needed
options.explanation: ATP is recycled through the ATP–ADP cycle, not made from scratch each time.

options.text: It is produced only in plant cells and traded to animal cells for use
options.explanation: Both plant and animal cells produce and use their own ATP.

toLevel3.stem: How does the structure of ATP make it suitable for storing and releasing energy?

options.text: The bond between the second and third phosphate can be easily broken and reformed
options.explanation: This bond is relatively unstable, allowing quick release of energy, and can be reformed when energy is available.

options.text: The adenine base stores energy in its ring structure permanently without change
options.explanation: The energy is stored in the phosphate bonds, not in the adenine base.

options.text: The ribose sugar vibrates to generate heat energy whenever the cell needs warmth
options.explanation: The ribose sugar is a structural component; energy release comes from breaking phosphate bonds.

options.text: All three phosphate groups must be removed simultaneously to release any energy
options.explanation: Typically only the third phosphate is removed to release energy, converting ATP to ADP.

toLevel3.stem: Why can't cells simply use glucose directly as an energy source for all cellular processes?

options.text: Glucose contains too much energy to power individual reactions efficiently
options.explanation: Glucose stores a large amount of energy; ATP provides energy in small, manageable packets suited to individual reactions.

options.text: Glucose cannot cross the plasma membrane under any circumstances whatsoever
options.explanation: Glucose does enter cells via transport proteins; the issue is that it is too energy-rich for direct use.

options.text: Glucose is only found in plant cells and animal cells cannot access it at all
options.explanation: Animal cells obtain glucose from food; the issue is that ATP provides energy in more usable amounts.

options.text: Glucose is identical to ATP in structure so there would be no benefit
options.explanation: Glucose and ATP are structurally very different molecules with different roles.

toLevel3.stem: What is the relationship between cellular respiration and the ATP–ADP cycle?

options.text: Respiration provides the energy to reform ATP from ADP and phosphate
options.explanation: The energy released from breaking down glucose during respiration is used to reattach phosphate to ADP, reforming ATP.

options.text: Respiration breaks down ATP to produce glucose for the cell to consume
options.explanation: Respiration breaks down glucose, not ATP; ATP is the product, not the substrate.

options.text: The ATP–ADP cycle replaces cellular respiration entirely in active cells
options.explanation: The ATP–ADP cycle depends on respiration to supply the energy needed to reform ATP.

options.text: Cellular respiration and the ATP–ADP cycle are completely independent processes
options.explanation: They are directly linked; respiration provides the energy that drives ATP reformation.

toLevel3.stem: Why is the conversion of ATP to ADP described as an exergonic reaction?

options.text: Because it releases energy when the phosphate bond is broken
options.explanation: Exergonic reactions release energy; breaking the terminal phosphate bond of ATP releases energy for cellular use.

options.text: Because it requires a large input of energy to proceed forward at all
options.explanation: A reaction requiring energy input is endergonic, not exergonic.

options.text: Because it only occurs at very high temperatures inside the cell
options.explanation: ATP breakdown occurs at body temperature with the help of enzymes; it does not require high temperatures.

options.text: Because it absorbs light energy from the environment to drive the process
options.explanation: ATP breakdown does not require light; it is an energy-releasing reaction.

toLevel3.stem: How does the reformation of ATP from ADP differ energetically from its breakdown?

options.text: Reformation requires energy input while breakdown releases energy
options.explanation: Adding a phosphate to ADP is endergonic (requires energy), while breaking ATP to ADP is exergonic (releases energy).

options.text: Both processes release equal amounts of energy in opposite directions
options.explanation: Reformation requires energy input; it does not release energy.

options.text: Reformation releases more energy than breakdown because it creates a stronger bond
options.explanation: Reformation stores energy in the bond; it does not release energy.

options.text: There is no energetic difference because both are spontaneous reactions naturally
options.explanation: ATP reformation is not spontaneous; it requires energy input from processes like respiration.

toLevel3.stem: The energy released from cellular respiration is used to reattach a phosphate group to ADP, reforming ATP.

options.text: True
options.explanation: Cellular respiration provides the energy needed to phosphorylate ADP back into ATP.

options.text: False
options.explanation: This statement correctly describes how respiration drives ATP reformation.

toLevel3.stem: ATP is called the energy currency because it provides energy in {{blank:1}} packets that can be used to power {{blank:2}} cellular processes.

options.text: small, manageable
options.explanation: ATP releases a controlled amount of energy suited to powering individual reactions.

options.text: large, uncontrolled
options.explanation: ATP provides energy in small, controlled amounts, not large uncontrolled bursts.

options.text: permanent, fixed
options.explanation: ATP energy is released temporarily and the molecule is recycled, not permanently fixed.

options.text: individual
options.explanation: ATP powers specific reactions one at a time with appropriate energy amounts.

options.text: no
options.explanation: ATP powers many cellular processes; it is the universal energy carrier.

options.text: only plant
options.explanation: ATP is used in all living cells, not just plant cells.

toLevel3.stem: The conversion of ATP to ADP is {{blank:1}} because it releases energy, while reforming ATP from ADP is {{blank:2}} because it requires energy.

options.text: exergonic
options.explanation: Exergonic reactions release energy; ATP breakdown releases energy for cellular use.

options.text: endergonic
options.explanation: Endergonic reactions require energy input; ATP breakdown releases energy.

options.text: isothermic
options.explanation: Isothermic is not the standard term; the correct term is exergonic.

options.text: endergonic
options.explanation: Endergonic reactions require energy input; ATP reformation requires energy from respiration.

options.text: exergonic
options.explanation: Exergonic reactions release energy; ATP reformation requires energy input.

options.text: spontaneous
options.explanation: ATP reformation is not spontaneous; it requires energy input.

toLevel3.stem: Cells cannot use glucose directly because it contains too much {{blank:1}} for individual reactions, so they convert it into {{blank:2}} instead.

options.text: energy
options.explanation: Glucose stores a large amount of energy that must be parcelled out via ATP for individual reactions.

options.text: protein
options.explanation: Glucose is a carbohydrate, not a protein; the issue is its energy content.

options.text: water
options.explanation: The issue is not water content; glucose has too much energy for direct use in individual reactions.

options.text: ATP
options.explanation: Cells convert the energy from glucose into many ATP molecules for use in individual reactions.

options.text: DNA
options.explanation: DNA stores genetic information, not energy; cells convert glucose energy into ATP.

options.text: starch
options.explanation: Starch is a storage form of glucose, not the energy currency used for cellular reactions.

toLevel4.stem: A muscle cell uses large amounts of ATP during contraction. What happens to the ADP produced?

options.text: It is recycled back to ATP using energy from cellular respiration
options.explanation: ADP is phosphorylated back to ATP using energy from glucose breakdown during respiration.

options.text: It is excreted from the cell as a waste product through the membrane
options.explanation: ADP is not a waste product; it is recycled into ATP within the cell.

options.text: It accumulates permanently inside the cell without ever being reused
options.explanation: ADP is continuously recycled back to ATP; it does not accumulate permanently.

options.text: It is converted directly into glucose for long-term energy storage
options.explanation: ADP is not converted into glucose; it is rephosphorylated to reform ATP.

toLevel4.stem: A cell is treated with a chemical that prevents phosphate groups from being added to ADP. What effect would this have?

options.text: The cell would run out of ATP and energy-requiring processes would stop
options.explanation: Without the ability to reform ATP from ADP, the cell's ATP supply would be depleted and all energy-dependent processes would cease.

options.text: The cell would function normally because it can use ADP as an energy source
options.explanation: ADP cannot substitute for ATP; cells require ATP for energy-dependent processes.

options.text: The cell would produce twice as much ATP to compensate for the blockage
options.explanation: The chemical blocks ATP reformation entirely; the cell cannot compensate.

options.text: The cell would switch to using glucose directly for all its energy needs
options.explanation: Cells cannot use glucose directly for individual reactions; ATP is required as an intermediary.

toLevel4.stem: During active transport, a membrane protein uses ATP to move ions against their concentration gradient. Which part of the ATP molecule provides the energy?

options.text: The bond between the second and third phosphate group
options.explanation: Breaking this bond releases energy that the transport protein uses to move ions against the gradient.

options.text: The adenine base at the core of the molecule
options.explanation: The adenine base is a structural component; the energy comes from the phosphate bond.

options.text: The ribose sugar that connects the base to the phosphates
options.explanation: The ribose sugar is structural; energy is released from the terminal phosphate bond.

options.text: The first phosphate group closest to the adenosine
options.explanation: Energy is released from the bond between the second and third phosphate, not the first.

toLevel4.stem: A scientist measures the rate of ATP consumption in different cell types. Which cell type would likely use the most ATP per hour?

options.text: A cardiac muscle cell that contracts continuously
options.explanation: Cardiac cells contract without rest, requiring a constant and high rate of ATP use.

options.text: A mature red blood cell circulating in the bloodstream passively
options.explanation: Mature red blood cells lack mitochondria and have relatively low energy demands.

options.text: A fat storage cell that remains mostly inactive in tissue
options.explanation: Fat storage cells have low metabolic activity and use relatively little ATP.

options.text: A bone cell embedded in the dense bone matrix structure
options.explanation: Bone cells have moderate metabolic activity, much less than continuously contracting muscle cells.

toLevel4.stem: A student suggests that eating more food should immediately increase the amount of ATP stored in cells. Why is this not accurate?

options.text: ATP is made and used rapidly; cells maintain a small working supply, not a large store
options.explanation: ATP is recycled thousands of times per day; cells keep only a small amount at any time rather than stockpiling it.

options.text: Food does not contain any energy that can be used to make ATP molecules at all
options.explanation: Food provides glucose and other substrates that are used in respiration to produce ATP.

options.text: ATP can only be made from sunlight through photosynthesis in plant cells only
options.explanation: All cells make ATP through cellular respiration; photosynthesis is one way to capture energy.

options.text: Cells have an unlimited supply of ATP that never needs to be replenished from food
options.explanation: Cells must continuously reform ATP; the supply is limited and requires energy from food.

toLevel4.stem: Nerve cells use ATP to maintain ion gradients across their membranes. If ATP production is inhibited, what is the immediate consequence?

options.text: Ion gradients dissipate because active transport pumps cannot function
options.explanation: Without ATP, sodium-potassium pumps cannot operate, and ion gradients collapse.

options.text: Ion gradients strengthen because passive diffusion speeds up significantly
options.explanation: Without active transport to maintain them, ion gradients would dissipate, not strengthen.

options.text: The nerve cell begins photosynthesis to generate its own ATP supply
options.explanation: Nerve cells cannot perform photosynthesis; they rely on cellular respiration for ATP.

options.text: Nothing changes because nerve cells do not use ATP for ion transport
options.explanation: Nerve cells heavily depend on ATP for active ion transport to maintain their function.

toLevel4.stem: An athlete's muscle cells produce ATP at a high rate during a sprint. What provides the energy to convert ADP back to ATP?

options.text: The breakdown of glucose through cellular respiration
options.explanation: Cellular respiration breaks down glucose and uses the released energy to phosphorylate ADP back to ATP.

options.text: The absorption of light energy by mitochondria during exercise
options.explanation: Mitochondria do not absorb light; energy comes from chemical breakdown of glucose.

options.text: The direct conversion of oxygen into chemical energy within cells
options.explanation: Oxygen is an electron acceptor in respiration; it is not directly converted into energy.

options.text: The physical movement of muscles generates electricity to reform ATP
options.explanation: Muscle movement uses ATP; it does not generate electricity to reform it.

toLevel4.stem: During muscle contraction, ATP is broken down to {{blank:1}}, and the energy released powers the {{blank:2}} of muscle fibres.

options.text: ADP and Pi
options.explanation: ATP loses its terminal phosphate to become ADP and inorganic phosphate (Pi).

options.text: glucose and CO₂
options.explanation: Glucose and CO₂ are involved in respiration, not the direct breakdown of ATP.

options.text: two ATP molecules
options.explanation: ATP does not split into two ATP molecules; it breaks down into ADP and Pi.

options.text: contraction
options.explanation: The energy from ATP hydrolysis directly powers the sliding of muscle filaments.

options.text: growth
options.explanation: Muscle growth is a longer-term process; ATP directly powers contraction.

options.text: digestion
options.explanation: Digestion occurs in the digestive system; ATP in muscle cells powers contraction.

toLevel4.stem: If a drug blocks the reformation of ATP, a cell's {{blank:1}} supply would be depleted and {{blank:2}} processes would stop.

options.text: ATP
options.explanation: Without reformation, the existing ATP would be used up and not replaced.

options.text: glucose
options.explanation: Glucose supply is not directly affected by blocking ATP reformation.

options.text: oxygen
options.explanation: Oxygen supply is unrelated to the reformation of ATP from ADP.

options.text: energy-requiring
options.explanation: Without ATP, active transport, muscle contraction, and other energy-dependent processes would cease.

options.text: all passive
options.explanation: Passive processes like diffusion do not require ATP and would continue.

options.text: photosynthetic
options.explanation: Most cells do not perform photosynthesis; the main impact is on energy-requiring processes.

toLevel4.stem: Cardiac muscle cells require large amounts of ATP because they {{blank:1}} continuously, so they contain many {{blank:2}} to produce it.

options.text: contract
options.explanation: The heart beats without rest, requiring constant ATP for muscle contraction.

options.text: divide
options.explanation: Cardiac muscle cells rarely divide; their high ATP demand is for contraction.

options.text: photosynthesise
options.explanation: Cardiac cells do not photosynthesise; they contract continuously.

options.text: mitochondria
options.explanation: Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration, which produces most of the cell's ATP.

options.text: chloroplasts
options.explanation: Chloroplasts are found in plant cells for photosynthesis, not in cardiac muscle.

options.text: ribosomes
options.explanation: Ribosomes produce proteins, not ATP.

toLevel5.stem: A cell typically contains only about 250 g of ATP at any moment, yet uses approximately 40 kg of ATP per day. What does this reveal about the ATP–ADP cycle?

options.text: Each ATP molecule must be recycled thousands of times per day
options.explanation: The huge daily ATP usage compared to the small pool means each molecule is rapidly broken down and reformed many times.

options.text: The cell stores most of its ATP outside the membrane for later use
options.explanation: ATP is used and recycled within the cell; it is not stored externally.

options.text: The cell manufactures entirely new ATP molecules each time rather than recycling them
options.explanation: The cell recycles ADP back to ATP; creating new molecules from scratch would be far too slow.

options.text: ATP usage data must be incorrect because such rapid turnover is biologically impossible
options.explanation: This rapid turnover is well documented and demonstrates the efficiency of the ATP–ADP cycle.

toLevel5.stem: A student claims that ATP is the only form of energy used in cells. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Incorrect; cells also use GTP, NADH, and other energy carriers for specific processes
options.explanation: While ATP is the primary energy currency, cells use other molecules like GTP, NADH, and FADH₂ for specific functions.

options.text: Correct; ATP is the sole energy molecule and no other carriers exist in any cell
options.explanation: Other energy carriers such as GTP and NADH play important roles in cellular processes.

options.text: Incorrect; cells primarily use glucose directly and ATP is only a minor side product
options.explanation: ATP is the primary energy currency; glucose is broken down to produce ATP, not used directly.

options.text: Correct; all cellular energy is stored exclusively in the phosphate bonds of ATP
options.explanation: Energy is also stored in molecules like NADH and FADH₂, which drive the electron transport chain.

toLevel5.stem: Why would a poison that mimics the structure of phosphate groups be particularly dangerous to cells?

options.text: It could block ATP reformation by competing with real phosphate for binding to ADP
options.explanation: A phosphate mimic could occupy the binding site on ADP, preventing the attachment of a real phosphate and halting ATP production.

options.text: It would cause cells to produce unlimited ATP leading to dangerous energy overload
options.explanation: A phosphate mimic would block ATP formation, not increase it.

options.text: It would strengthen the phosphate bonds in ATP making them impossible to ever break
options.explanation: A mimic would interfere with ATP reformation, not strengthen existing bonds.

options.text: It would have no effect because phosphate groups are not important to ATP at all
options.explanation: Phosphate groups are essential to ATP function; disrupting them would be lethal.

toLevel5.stem: Some organisms in deep-sea hydrothermal vents use chemosynthesis instead of photosynthesis. How does this relate to ATP production?

options.text: Chemosynthesis provides an alternative energy source to drive ATP reformation from ADP
options.explanation: These organisms use chemical energy from inorganic compounds instead of light to produce ATP via the same fundamental cycle.

options.text: These organisms do not use ATP at all because they evolved a completely different system
options.explanation: All known living organisms use ATP; the difference is the energy source, not the energy currency.

options.text: Chemosynthesis produces a different molecule called CTP that replaces ATP entirely
options.explanation: CTP exists but is not the energy currency; these organisms still use ATP.

options.text: Deep-sea organisms absorb ATP directly from the water surrounding hydrothermal vents
options.explanation: Organisms produce their own ATP; they do not absorb it from the environment.

toLevel5.stem: During intense exercise, ATP is consumed faster than aerobic respiration can supply it. What happens in the cell?

options.text: Anaerobic pathways supplement ATP production but yield far less ATP per glucose
options.explanation: When aerobic respiration cannot keep pace, anaerobic fermentation provides rapid but less efficient ATP production.

options.text: The cell stops all activity until aerobic respiration catches up to the demand level
options.explanation: Cells do not simply stop; they switch to anaerobic pathways to maintain some ATP supply.

options.text: The cell begins photosynthesis to supplement its ATP supply during intense exercise
options.explanation: Animal cells cannot perform photosynthesis; they rely on anaerobic respiration during high demand.

options.text: ATP molecules are imported from resting cells through gap junctions to the active cells
options.explanation: ATP is generally not transferred between cells; each cell produces its own.

toLevel5.stem: A researcher proposes replacing ATP with a synthetic molecule that releases more energy per bond. What potential problems might arise?

options.text: Enzymes evolved to use ATP's specific energy release would not function with a different molecule
options.explanation: Cellular enzymes are precisely adapted to the energy released by ATP hydrolysis; a different energy level could damage or fail to drive reactions.

options.text: No problems would arise because any molecule that releases energy can substitute for ATP
options.explanation: Enzymes require specific energy amounts; too much or too little would disrupt cellular processes.

options.text: The synthetic molecule would be better in every way because more energy is always beneficial
options.explanation: Enzymes require precise energy inputs; excess energy could denature proteins or cause damaging side reactions.

options.text: The cell would simply adapt its enzymes overnight to use the new energy molecule
options.explanation: Enzyme adaptation requires evolutionary change over many generations, not overnight adjustment.

toLevel5.stem: Comparing a hibernating bear to an active bear, how would ATP turnover rates differ and why?

options.text: The active bear has much higher ATP turnover because of greater metabolic demands
options.explanation: Active movement, body heat maintenance, and cellular processes require far more ATP cycling than the reduced metabolism of hibernation.

options.text: Both bears have identical ATP turnover because all mammals use ATP at the same rate
options.explanation: ATP turnover varies dramatically with metabolic activity; hibernating animals have much lower rates.

options.text: The hibernating bear has higher turnover because it must store extra ATP for awakening
options.explanation: Hibernation involves reduced metabolism and lower ATP turnover; ATP is not stockpiled.

options.text: Neither bear uses significant amounts of ATP because bears rely on fat reserves instead
options.explanation: Fat reserves are broken down to produce ATP; both bears use ATP, but at different rates.

toLevel5.stem: A student argues that the ATP–ADP cycle is an example of a coupled reaction. Evaluate this claim.

options.text: Correct; the exergonic breakdown of ATP is coupled to endergonic cellular processes
options.explanation: The energy released from ATP hydrolysis drives endergonic reactions that would not occur spontaneously.

options.text: Incorrect; ATP breakdown and cellular processes are completely independent reactions
options.explanation: ATP hydrolysis is directly coupled to energy-requiring processes; they are not independent.

options.text: Correct; but only because both reactions occur in the same organelle at the same time
options.explanation: Coupling refers to energy transfer between reactions, not merely their co-location.

options.text: Incorrect; coupled reactions only occur in non-living chemical systems outside of cells
options.explanation: Coupled reactions are fundamental to biochemistry and occur extensively in living cells.

toLevel5.stem: The fact that cells contain only a small amount of ATP yet use kilograms daily demonstrates that each ATP molecule is {{blank:1}} at an extremely high rate.

options.text: recycled
options.explanation: The rapid turnover means each ATP molecule is broken down to ADP and reformed many times per day.

options.text: destroyed
options.explanation: ATP is not destroyed; it is recycled through the ATP–ADP cycle.

options.text: accumulated
options.explanation: ATP is not accumulated; it is used and reformed continuously.

toLevel5.stem: The ATP–ADP cycle is a coupled reaction because the {{blank:1}} reaction of ATP breakdown drives {{blank:2}} reactions in the cell.

options.text: exergonic
options.explanation: ATP breakdown releases energy (exergonic), which is used to power other reactions.

options.text: endergonic
options.explanation: ATP breakdown releases energy; endergonic reactions require energy input.

options.text: isothermic
options.explanation: Isothermic is not the correct term; ATP breakdown is exergonic.

options.text: endergonic
options.explanation: The energy from ATP drives endergonic reactions that require energy input.

options.text: exergonic
options.explanation: Exergonic reactions release energy; it is the endergonic reactions that need ATP energy.

options.text: spontaneous
options.explanation: Spontaneous reactions do not require energy input; ATP drives non-spontaneous (endergonic) reactions.
